# What the Architect Owns {#sec-what-architect-owns}

::: {.epigraph}
> "The second irony is that the designer who tries to eliminate the operator still leaves the operator to do the tasks which the designer cannot think how to automate."
>
> — Lisanne Bainbridge, *Ironies of Automation* [@Bainbridge1983Ironies, p. 775]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *If AI can perform substantial design work, what do architects still contribute and remain responsible for?*

**Core thesis:** *Architectural ownership resides in framing problems, setting abstractions, judging cross-layer trade-offs, and governing commitment to silicon.*
:::

If an autonomous system could generate millions of register-transfer level (RTL) lines, sweep thousands of microarchitectural configurations, and close physical timing without human intervention, what would be left for the architect to own? Even as frontier models increasingly help propose problem formulations and abstractions, the architect remains responsible for the work that decides what the automation is for: framing the problem that matches product reality, setting the abstractions and the system boundary, judging the cross-layer trade-offs that no single tool observes, and preparing the recommendation on which an accountable person commits silicon. That final commitment is never a formality, because a leading-edge mask set alone is estimated in the tens of millions of dollars [@Patel2022MaskSetCosts], and authorizing fabrication spends that capital before any wafer is measured.

Because the stakes of fabrication are so high, measuring a complete system against matched baselines and adversarial challenges (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect) is only part of the discipline. Architectural ownership also draws a structural line between exploring candidate implementations and authorizing irreversible commitments (@fig-ch11-cover-map). It separates a *technical recommendation* (an evidence-grounded assessment of whether a candidate design works) from *commitment authority* (the organizational decision to tape out, freeze an interface, or accept residual risk). When automation takes over routine implementation, the architect's primary duty shifts from drafting hardware to questioning what the tools report. A clean timing report, for example, may rest on a false-path exception that nobody justified, and the architect must be able to find it.

![**Architectural ownership separates candidate evaluation from commitment authority.** An AI-native design system and domain specialists explore candidate spaces and verify implementations, but architects own problem formulation, abstraction boundaries, and cross-layer trade-offs. The resulting system recommendation provides qualified evidence to an authorized organizational decision maker rather than committing resources automatically.](images/ch11-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch11-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which substantial AI-native design work and architectural ownership remain distinct from a named commitment authority inside an accountable organization."}

This division keeps technical exploration anchored in an accountable organization. While domain specialists and automated generators explore candidate designs within the bounds of their assigned tools, they cannot widen their own scope or prove that the pieces work together across layers. The architect therefore reconciles those specialist and tool findings, surfaces the physical interactions they left out, and states the remaining risk plainly so that the resulting recommendation gives an authorized human decision maker an inspectable basis to advance, hold, or reject the candidate. Nor does ownership end at tapeout. Runtime monitoring and shifting operational assumptions feed back directly into the architectural record, providing explicit triggers to reopen commitments when physical reality departs from the evaluated models.

## Delegating Without Losing Technical Contact {#sec-delegating-without-losing-contact}

Keeping exploration and commitment separate requires a deliberate balance: architects must delegate large portions of implementation without losing technical contact with the hardware. As Fred Brooks observed, the essential difficulty of engineering lies in specifying system intent and boundaries [@Brooks1986NoSilverBullet]. An automated system may help formulate a problem or propose a better one, but the people responsible for the product must decide whether that is the problem worth solving. In the governance model proposed here, an automated design system can synthesize candidates, run verification suites, and assemble a *technical recommendation*: an inspectable packet of evidence showing whether a candidate design satisfies its declared formal, timing, thermal, and functional constraints. *Commitment authority* stays with an accountable human decision maker who authorizes reticle mask fabrication, freezes an interface, or accepts residual risk on behalf of the organization. Neither responsibility depends on assuming that human design proposals are always better; the separation exists because a software system cannot bear financial or engineering accountability when silicon fails.

In conventional workflows, engineers build the judgment needed to evaluate a recommendation by writing RTL, inspecting waveforms, and iterating with electronic design automation (EDA) tools, where they see directly how microarchitectural choices turn into routing congestion and timing slack. When a team delegates candidate drafting, macro floorplanning, and regression sweeps to automated loops, that point of contact shifts. The architect need not repeat every automated step by hand, but must still be able to inspect the specific traces, floorplans, and assumptions that could overturn the recommendation.

Four questions help determine how much work can be delegated and what must be checked before acting on its results:

1. **Observability**: can the architect inspect the candidate, its evaluation conditions, and the traces supporting the recommendation?
2. **Reversibility**: which changes can be rolled back cleanly, and which would require costly rework once accepted?
3. **Independent checks**: what checks could expose errors in the proposal or its evaluation, and which assumptions do those checks share with the automated loop?
4. **Bounded consequences**: which cross-layer effects have been evaluated, and which remain outside the study's scope?

How an engineering team answers these four questions depends on the operational layer governing the workflow (@sec-three-operational-layers, @fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration).

In a Layer 1 workflow, the human engineer keeps direct line-level contact with the design. Generative models propose isolated leaf implementations, such as an arithmetic block or a testbench harness, while the engineer retains the structural design choices, sets all interface protocols, and integrates the modules by hand. Here the four questions have direct answers: observability comes from reading the source code, reversibility is a routine version-control rollback, and the human engineer remains individually accountable for functional correctness.

In a Layer 2 workflow, the architect freezes the structural container $\Theta$, including permitted template choices and external interfaces, and delegates parameter exploration $\theta \in \Theta$ across cache capacities, unroll factors, or floorplan coordinates to an automated optimizer. Learned macro placement, the method later named AlphaChip, is the best-known example, and whether its reported gains hold against strong conventional placers remains disputed [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @GoldieEtAl2024ThatChipHasSailed; @ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment]. Once the search moves from source lines to parameter vectors and objective functions, rolling back a poor search region requires tightening parameter bounds, while verification centers on testing surrogate model fidelity and preventing the optimizer from gaming a proxy metric at the expense of unmodeled congestion.

At Layer 3, public evidence remains thin. A public end-to-end report, examined in @sec-design-conductor-case, carries a short specification to layout but reports no matched baseline, so the demands such a system places on ownership remain largely prospective. If a design system were permitted to open the structural container and generate alternative microarchitectures, specialized memory hierarchies, and compiler lowering schedules together, line-by-line human inspection of the generated RTL would stop being a practical primary check. Observability would instead depend on formal contract satisfaction, cross-layer execution traces, and physical signoff metrics. Reversibility would require strict execution sandboxes that keep production constraint files read-only, while verification accountability would shift from manual code review to qualifying the formal properties, physical signoff checks, and pre-silicon derating envelopes themselves.

Across all three layers, these questions are relatively straightforward to answer during a bounded array-mapping sweep or focused tool run whose state, checks, and side effects stay confined to one block. They become much harder when a decision locks in interfaces across the stack. Freezing an instruction set architecture (ISA) contract or fixing the physical layer (PHY) lane count on a 2.5D Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) link[^fn-ucie-phy-c11] hardens assumptions across compiler runtimes, memory hierarchies, RTL, floorplans, and product thermals at once. Before the responsible lead authorizes such a freeze, the architect must reconcile evidence across every one of those coupled layers.

[^fn-ucie-phy-c11]: **Die-to-die physical layers and interconnect budgeting**: In multi-die systems, Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) defines standard physical layer (PHY) lane allocations, die-edge beachfront reach, and bump pitches (typically $100\text{--}130\ \mu\text{m}$ for standard organic package substrates and $25\text{--}55\ \mu\text{m}$ for advanced 2.5D packaging such as silicon interposers or bridges). Freezing PHY lane counts constrains die-edge allocation, substrate routing layers, and escape routing. Bandwidth can still change through supported link rates within the qualified operating envelope; adding lanes or exceeding those capabilities may require an expensive package redesign. [@UCIeConsortium2024Overview]

Reconciling those layers requires direct technical contact across tool boundaries, where human-factors research distinguishes *misuse* (inappropriate reliance on automation) from *disuse* (neglecting automation capabilities entirely) [@ParasuramanRiley1997HumansAutomation]. Although logic synthesis and hardware construction languages provide powerful abstractions for expressing and implementing designs [@DeMicheli1994SynthesisOptimization; @Izraelevitz2017Chisel], engineers working through any abstraction still need ways to challenge the problem formulation, inspect decisive failure traces, and recognize physical effects the model omits. Once automated loops absorb routine microarchitectural sweeps and propose broader redesigns, architects rely on that diagnostic access to identify missing constraints, develop cross-layer alternatives, and judge whether the combined evidence supports a system recommendation.

The same delegation creates an apprenticeship risk. Junior engineers who encounter designs only through prompts and scorecards may miss the diagnostic experience needed to challenge a result or recommend a consequential change. Teaching that judgment requires deliberate opportunities to investigate failures; @sec-curriculum-certification considers how a curriculum could provide them.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Judgment Precedes and Governs Automation"}
**The principle:** Automation may formulate problems, explore alternatives, implement designs, and analyze systems. Architects must retain the technical understanding needed to challenge and revise the problem, the abstraction, and the system boundaries as results emerge.

**The application:** A review supporting a commitment should explain how the component results support one feasible system recommendation and what evidence could overturn it. It should identify the architect responsible for that recommendation and the commitment authority responsible for the organizational decision.
:::

## Framing Cross-Layer Problems {#sec-framing-architecture-problem}

An architect puts that principle to work first by framing the problem that an automated design loop will explore. Framing the problem means defining the system boundary, identifying the governing cross-layer interactions, and deciding which physical consequences the evaluation must measure, then revisiting those choices when generated candidates and tool runs reveal missing constraints or better organizations. Because the choice of mechanisms, interfaces, and fallback strategies frames the design space itself [@PattersonDitzel1980RISC], the architect's role extends beyond bounding the physical hardware to designing the decision workflow: selecting methods to propose candidate modifications, modeling tools to estimate properties, validation checks to screen candidates, and ways to investigate cross-layer disagreements.

In @sec-intent-vs-spec, we decomposed the Lighthouse XR specification request, "Design a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for a real-time mobile extended-reality (XR) workload," across eight requirement domains. Consider a candidate organization that combines a central processing unit (CPU) with a neural processing unit (NPU) across a UCIe packaging link. That template is one possible organization rather than a choice settled by the request, and how deeply the team must evaluate it depends on the commitment at stake.

A freeze decision asks far more of the requirement decomposition than a local exploration does: whereas studying array utilization requires only cycle-level modeling and mapping search, freezing that array alongside its software interface and packaging link demands evidence that the selected parts work together as a subsystem. Before recommending a freeze, the architect must connect compiler lowering through Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) to the memory traffic it produces and check whether the resulting execution meets timing and stays within the total 3\ W subsystem thermal design power (TDP) limit. While IP review and non-recurring engineering (NRE) capital review add organizational conditions for proceeding, the specific architecture question determines which technical models and checks must run to support the recommendation.

Across decisions of this kind, eight recurring judgments help turn isolated tool results into one coherent recommendation (@tbl-architect-technical-judgments). Together they help the architect surface missing constraints, resolve cross-layer trade-offs, and state residual risk plainly, giving the commitment decision a physically grounded account of the system and its remaining uncertainties.

| **Judgment** | **Architectural question** | **Lighthouse consequence** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Problem choice and reframing** | Is the stated problem still the one the product needs solved? | Deciding whether the goal is maximizing raw NPU general matrix multiply (GEMM) utilization or meeting the proposed 120\ frames per second (FPS) mobile XR operating point and its workload-specific deadlines within a 3\ W TDP envelope. |
| **Abstraction** | Which details can be simplified for this decision? | A cycle-level NPU model can compare matrix mappings locally, but it cannot hide Triton/LLVM/MLIR compiler lowering, static random-access memory (SRAM) / LPDDR5 memory traffic, UCIe interconnect energy, physical timing, or the 3\ W subsystem boundary from a freeze decision. |
| **System boundary** | Where do workload, software, hardware, package, physical design, and product effects meet? | Deciding whether NPU array sizing can be analyzed in isolation, or must encompass host 64-bit RISC-V application core with vector extensions (RV64GCV) task dispatch, UCIe chiplet routing, dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) bandwidth contention, and packaging thermal limits. |
| **Architecture synthesis** | Do chosen mechanisms, interfaces, software paths, and implementation choices form one feasible system? | Confirming that the NPU matrix engine, RV64GCV CPU contract, compiler lowering pipeline, LPDDR5 memory subsystem, and firmware fallback paths form a coherent, manufacturable subsystem. |
| **Missing constraints** | What has the formulation, representation, or tool path left out? | Uncovering omitted physical and legal factors: transient power delivery network (PDN) voltage droop ($di/dt$), 3\ W thermal dissipation limits, UCIe signal integrity, IP indemnification, and hardware chicken-bit fallbacks. |
| **Cross-layer trade-off** | Which feasible point best serves the product when objectives conflict? | Resolving the tension between host RV64GCV vector tail latency, NPU matrix throughput, LPDDR5 memory power, UCIe die-to-die routing congestion, and manual review burden. |
| **Mechanism and consequence** | Does the proposed explanation fit the observations, and what happens if it is wrong? | Evaluating whether an apparent speedup is driven by architectural dataflow or an unmodeled memory wait state, where an erroneous tapeout freeze risks multimillion-dollar silicon mask respins. |
| **Commitment under uncertainty** | Are remaining risks understood, containable, and worth accepting? | Recommending against physical tapeout when static timing closure, formal property bounds, IP indemnification, and power delivery margins remain uncharacterized. |
: **Architecture judgment gives technical work its system meaning.** Architects choose the question, abstraction, boundary, and consequence before the commitment authority decides whether the design advances. {#tbl-architect-technical-judgments tbl-colwidths="[22,38,40]"}

In practice, these eight judgments expose where a feasibility claim rests on physical coupling that individual models left out. Reconciling a 120\ FPS XR rendering target with a 3\ W thermal envelope, for example, requires tracing how NPU direct memory access (DMA) burst sizing affects LPDDR5 bus contention, host CPU interrupt latency, and package thermal gradients before committing to tapeout. In our hypothetical CPU-NPU-UCIe candidate, those effects remain open questions to investigate rather than demonstrated properties of a feasible subsystem. Because simplified abstractions routinely hide bottlenecks that cross block boundaries, identifying those interactions early tells the architect which models are safe to trust and which additional implementation checks the recommendation needs.

## Selecting System Abstractions and Bounds {#sec-selecting-abstractions-constraints}

Once the system boundaries are set, the architect chooses the representations and analytical models that govern exploration, recognizing that every architectural model is defined as much by what it omits as by what it represents. While a memory trace in Ramulator can expose channel contention and an NPU dataflow model in SCALE-Sim shows how a mapping occupies the array, neither view alone establishes physical timing or thermal feasibility. Moving to RTL simulation, physical implementation tools, and a package thermal model adds those physical observations, but it also creates a reconciliation problem because the workload, interfaces, and operating conditions must agree across every view. When the architect selects an abstraction, the task therefore includes naming the omitted details that could flip the decision and scheduling a check that can observe them.

::: {.column-margin}
**Architecture description standards.** ISO/IEC/Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 42010 distinguishes an entity architecture from an architecture description that expresses it. The standard specifies requirements for architecture viewpoints and model kinds, but it does not prescribe this book's chapter structure, a team's specific design process, or the organizational assignment of commitment authority [@ISOIECIEEE2022ArchitectureDescription].
:::

Choosing an abstraction also fixes what architectural state each predictor, generator, optimizer, or tool is allowed to modify and which measurements constrain those edits. Combining locally optimized blocks will not yield a working chip when internal abstractions omit blocking physical effects such as power delivery network (PDN) voltage droop or die-to-die thermal coupling. Consider a learned macro placer such as AlphaChip [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]: if a team configured a hypothetical NPU placement objective that omitted power-grid and package-thermal effects, the optimizer could return a favorable placement score without establishing that neighboring CPU cores retain adequate supply voltage or that the combined package meets its thermal limit. Those physical consequences require separate checks, not because of any reported failure in AlphaChip itself, but because the objective function never measured them. Because a generator given direct control over standard-cell placement likewise requires checks for foundry design rules, well spacing, and available routing tracks, the architect must define block boundaries, curate macro sets, set timing and power constraints across host CPU and NPU cores, choose comparison baselines, and arrange physical signoff.

Omitted constraints become even more hazardous once an automated system is allowed to open the structural container. When an optimizer is confined to a fixed template and none of its permitted parameter choices relieves a saturated memory interface, the search simply stalls at the boundary of that template. A system allowed to alter topologies across software, microarchitecture, and circuits has no fixed template to confine what it proposes: without an explicit power-delivery model, for example, an optimizer could cluster high-activity vector units where transient supply droop threatens timing, and nothing in its objective would register the problem. In such a workflow, the architect's responsibility shifts from curating local parameter bounds to ensuring that every governing physical invariant is enforced in the signoff checks.

Beyond choosing models for individual tools, architects govern how components interact by defining interface contracts, assigning revision authority, selecting independent signoff checks, and auditing shared assumptions across verification steps. Many consequential constraints originate as unwritten engineering experience [@Polanyi1966TacitDimension, p. 4]: compiler leads may know that a proposed matrix opcode lacks an efficient lowering path, while physical-design leads recognize power-grid heuristics that break down on dense CPU-NPU floorplans. Language models can help locate, compare, and organize these scattered expert judgments for formal review, but any constraint that shapes the design still requires verification checks matched to its risk and scope, whether run by automated checkers, conventional EDA tools, domain specialists, or peer reviewers.

Once the team accepts such a constraint, the architectural record should state its source, its scope, the interfaces it affects, its known conflicts, and the conditions that would reopen it. Suppose a physical designer's rule bars placing two high-current macros on the same power stripe for a given metal stack and operating threshold; the architect decides how to enforce that rule in the floorplanner and evaluates the resulting routing overhead. If the project later moves to a new power-grid template or a 3D stacked die, the physical assumptions behind that rule no longer hold, triggering a fresh review rather than leaving an obsolete restriction in force. Recording both the constraint and its operating assumptions keeps an optimizer from quietly violating unwritten physical limits without rejecting valid designs when the technology changes.

## Governing System Integration {#sec-orchestrating-system-integration}

Setting clean abstractions and constraints prepares the ground for the next job of ownership: integrating specialist and tool outputs into a single working system. A design candidate becomes a viable architecture, rather than an assortment of isolated optimizations, only when its mechanisms and interfaces hold together under the physical and logical conditions of the full stack. Automated methods can reason across layers when those interactions are represented and checked, but any result from a tool or domain specialist covers only the interactions its model includes. An NPU array optimization that omits host CPU cache coherence, memory channel contention, or UCIe chiplet thermal dissipation cannot establish feasibility across those boundaries; the architect has to set and challenge the scope of those studies, expose missing interactions, and compose specialized results into a unified system recommendation.

Consider a hypothetical revision of the Lighthouse XR system-on-chip (SoC). Trace analyses in gem5 and SCALE-Sim support the target frame rate, MLIR compiler searches yield legal NPU tiling, Verilator RTL simulations pass, Ramulator memory models satisfy local bandwidth checks, OpenSTA reports that timing constraints are met, and power-aware checks using Unified Power Format (UPF) verify the declared power-gating behavior. Although each check passes in isolation, combining the results exposes cross-layer faults: the burst memory traffic introduced by the new NPU tiling pushes estimated subsystem power across SRAM arrays, UCIe links, and LPDDR5 channels past the 3\ W thermal envelope, while a critical tail-latency path has no software fallback.

To resolve those faults, the architect proposes coordinated adjustments across the stack: assign tail-latency handling to the host CPU core, narrow NPU DMA bursts, rebalance memory buffers, and specify firmware fallback paths. Each adjustment creates a new cross-layer obligation of its own. Narrower bursts relieve memory contention at the expense of accelerator throughput and must be re-evaluated against the frame deadline; moving work to the host CPU requires checking its scheduling and power draw under concurrent load; and rebalancing buffers requires checking capacity and backpressure under the revised traffic pattern. The firmware fallback path must likewise preserve functional correctness with its latency and power costs measured under the conditions in which it runs, whereas programmable control-register overrides (often called *chicken-bits*) offer a post-silicon way to disable a faulty speculative path only if verification proves that flipping the override actually contains the fault. Working through these coupled checks turns a collection of local passes into a candidate system whose end-to-end interactions can be tested.

The resulting recommendation explains why the revised subsystem should meet its requirements and identifies any checks that still disagree. Those remaining disagreements deserve close attention before a preferred candidate advances, because they often expose a broken interface assumption that no single-domain optimization examined.

## Resolving Cross-Layer Discrepancies {#sec-resolving-discrepancies}

When models across different domains disagree, the conflict may expose incompatible assumptions, competing approximations, or a candidate that genuinely improves one metric while failing another requirement. If a cycle-level simulator reports performance gains for a new NPU array mapping while physical signoff tools report power-grid voltage droop under concurrent host CPU vector loads, both tools may be right, and the faster mapping is still infeasible under realistic system load. Because the architect cannot average those metrics or pick the more convenient report under schedule pressure to dismiss a blocking failure, architectural judgment begins by asking what each result actually establishes. Before the design can advance, the team must explain the physical mechanism behind the conflict, reexamine the model abstractions, run a check that separates the competing explanations, or hold the candidate until the blocking discrepancy is resolved.

Three steps help separate a candidate defect from a disagreement about what the tools checked:

1. **Contract and condition alignment**: The architect and domain specialists identify the requirement each check addresses and compare implementation versions, workloads, operating conditions, and assumptions. Checks of different requirements need not agree on whether a candidate is favorable. A valid failure of an applicable blocking requirement rules out the candidate under those conditions, even when another check passes.
2. **Abstraction correction**: When checks encode inconsistent assumptions or interfaces, determine which representation departs from the intended product contract. Correct the erroneous abstraction, model, or interface definition and rerun affected tool paths. If the contract itself is ambiguous, resolve its meaning against the product requirements before rerunning the checks; do not weaken a valid requirement to obtain a pass.
3. **Investigation of unresolved discrepancies**: When formal proofs and cycle-accurate models still disagree about an interface invariant, select an observation that can distinguish the competing explanations. If the discrepancy cannot be resolved within verification budgets, the candidate remains blocked from advancing past the affected check. The architect and affected specialists identify what remains unexplained before signoff.

Suppose a coherence verifier using SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) and bounded model checking (BMC) returns a counterexample within $k = 50$ cycles against a blocking property between host CPU caches and NPU DMA stores, while a high-level software model treats the same execution as legal under high-contention LPDDR5 traffic.[^fn-bmc-c11] Neither the architect nor an automated loop may weaken the property, discard the failing workload, or relabel the counterexample as passing; and when generative models propose both the candidate RTL and the formal assertions, verification engineers must derive the assertions independently or test the harness with mutation testing so the loop cannot confirm its own misread specification. To resolve the conflict between the formal check and the software model, we ask whether both tools encode the same product contract and permit the memory events in the counterexample. Tracing how the software model represents those exact memory events locates where the two views diverge. If the counterexample reflects behavior the candidate hardware can produce and violates a valid blocking requirement, the candidate fails; otherwise, the team corrects the erroneous representation or resolves the contract ambiguity and reruns both paths.

[^fn-bmc-c11]: **Bounded model checking and SystemVerilog Assertions**: SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) express formal properties to check. Bounded model checking (BMC) searches for a property violation within a specified number of unrolled execution cycles under encoded assumptions; a completed passing check establishes the absence of a counterexample within that finite bound, not an inductive proof at arbitrary depth [@SymbiYosys].

A different discrepancy arises when feasible candidates pass their blocking checks but return overlapping estimates for tail latency and subsystem power. Here the architect asks whether workload sampling, model error, or untested operating corners could flip which design wins. The right response is to run the least costly check with enough fidelity to separate the candidates on the specific uncertainty that could change the recommendation: matched cycle-level trace runs in gem5 for workload-dependent timing, physical thermal simulations for heat buildup, OpenSTA static timing runs for path slack, or post-layout power-grid analyses for voltage droop. If the available checks cannot resolve the overlap within budget, the architect keeps the recommendation narrow and favors choices that remain reversible.

## Separating Evidence from Commitments {#sec-linking-results-claims-commitments}

Resolving cross-layer discrepancies yields qualified evidence for a hardware recommendation, yet that hardware evidence answers a different question from whether the complete design approach improved architecture quality or reduced total engineering cost. A sound hardware candidate does not by itself establish a workflow advantage, and a workflow advantage does not prove that its candidate meets product requirements. Neither finding constitutes a decision to tape out silicon.

To connect hardware evidence to project governance, the architect assembles a recommendation that presents the preferred candidate alongside evaluated alternatives, explains the cross-layer trade-offs, documents boundary conditions and signoff checks, and states the remaining uncertainties. Domain specialists remain responsible for the validity and scope of their signoffs across timing closure, power integrity, physical implementation, and reliability, while the organization decides whether the supported recommendation justifies the next commitment.

The two independent tests from @sec-moonshot structure this separation:

1. **Evidence test (program claim)**: Did the complete approach improve the architecture result or reduce total cost to reach a comparable result? (Classified as *supported*, *unsupported*, or *unresolved*.)
2. **Decision test (architecture commitment)**: Do the people authorized to commit the project, weighing the architectural recommendation, trade-offs, result limits, and residual risk, decide that the work justifies the next transition?

Keeping these two tests separate makes program evaluation and architecture commitment independent. Even when a workflow claim is *supported*, demonstrating a faster search or a better Pareto frontier does not compel a silicon commitment if physical thermals, organizational capacity, or business risks remain unacceptable; conversely, an *unresolved* workflow comparison does not prevent an organization from committing to a sound hardware architecture backed by thorough physical signoff. Because an evidence status never records a product decision, every recommendation must identify who is authorized to approve the next transition and present the specific hardware evidence that transition requires.

## Governing Tapeout Commitments {#sec-governing-tapeout-commitments}

What a commitment requires depends on how much of the design the next transition locks in, as advancing from high-level exploration to physical silicon progressively freezes interfaces, bus contracts, and floorplans. Whereas modifying ISA extensions or buffer layouts early in the design cycle requires only editing software models or RTL, modifying package substrate routing and reticle masks after freeze can cost millions of dollars and months of delay [@Patel2022MaskSetCosts], so the supporting evidence must address the consequences that will become hardest to reverse.

::: {.callout-war-story title="An architecture can outlast its original product plan"}
**The architecture.** Larrabee described a many-core x86 architecture for visual computing, with wide vector units, coherent caches, and a software renderer in place of most fixed-function graphics hardware [@SeilerEtAl2008Larrabee]. In September 2009, Intel demonstrated Larrabee silicon and described plans for discrete graphics products [@Intel2009LarrabeeDemonstration].

**The later plan.** In May 2010, Intel announced Many Integrated Core product plans targeting high-performance computing and identified Larrabee as one of the projects from which the architecture was derived [@Intel2010MICPlans]. This chronology establishes architectural reuse under a different product plan. It does not disclose the complete internal evidence or capital-allocation rationale behind that plan.

**The lesson.** Reusing an architecture and committing to a particular product are different decisions. A recommendation must identify the target workload, product requirements, and remaining expenditure for the proposed transition. The people responsible for that product must decide whether to proceed; a published architecture or a working demonstration cannot supply that decision.
:::

That boundary between exploring a design and committing a product holds across all three operational layers. Execution rights widen with the layer, from leaf edits inside human-authored RTL, to parameter changes inside a frozen container, to rewriting interfaces, pipelines, and compiler passes in a system that restructures cross-layer topology, yet they always stop short of commitment. A generator with the authority to rewrite RTL across modules does not thereby gain authority to approve timing waivers, relax signoff constraints, or declare its own output tapeout-ready.

Separating execution from commitment requires a clear record of who decides what. Commitment records specify which design advances, which alternatives were rejected, which conditions the evidence covered, what uncertainty remains, and what triggers would reopen the choice. The division in @tbl-lighthouse-action-rights makes three responsibilities explicit: doing the design work, establishing what its results support, and deciding whether to commit. These responsibilities may involve overlapping teams, but completing one step never authorizes the next.

| **Decision** | **Technical question** | **Boundary** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Execute design work** | What candidate state may this person, model, or tool change, and when must it stop? | Work stays within the declared design space, interfaces, budget, and evaluator boundary. |
| **Establish what a result supports** | What does this check show about this artifact under these conditions and assumptions? | Domain specialists own result validity and domain scope. The architect determines how that result applies to the system decision. |
| **Commit the architecture** | Does the integrated design justify the next consequential transition (e.g., tapeout freeze)? | The named commitment authority decides after considering the architect's system recommendation, alternatives, cross-layer results, specialist concurrences, uncertainty, and residual risk. |
: **Execution, support, and commitment carry different responsibilities.** A successful tool run or a favorable local result cannot silently authorize a system architecture. {#tbl-lighthouse-action-rights tbl-colwidths="[28,34,38]"}

Classic human-automation frameworks distinguish information acquisition, analysis, decision selection, and action implementation [@ParasuramanEtAl2000LevelsAutomation]. Here, the distinction determines who may advance a candidate and on what basis.[^fn-kernel-maintainer-c11] A specialist's signoff enters the architect's recommendation; the named authority then records a decision against that recommendation. Completed check records remain immutable, so subsequent judgments cannot rewrite past results.

[^fn-kernel-maintainer-c11]: **Linux kernel review as a limited analogy**: Kernel submission guidance separates submission to the relevant maintainers, review, testing, and the Developer Certificate of Origin; `Signed-off-by:` records the contributor's certification of the right to submit or pass on the patch, not proof that it is correct [@LinuxKernelSubmittingPatches]. The useful parallel is separating a candidate proposal from its review and acceptance, not equating a maintainer's role or that contributor declaration with hardware signoff or tapeout responsibility.

Keeping completed check records immutable matters when operating conditions shift or new physical constraints emerge and make earlier results inapplicable. Rather than overwriting old measurements, the team appends fresh checks with their conditions and versions to preserve the basis of the original decision for later diagnosis, although record integrity makes that history inspectable rather than proving that the checks were sufficient or their assumptions correct.

### IP Provenance and Indemnification

Before committing capital to silicon fabrication, the organization must also resolve the IP conditions under which it can use the candidate. For generated RTL, the technical record should identify the supplied sources, permitted transformations, and checks performed. It must also expose what is unknown about the generator's training data or the origin of an emitted fragment, so those limits remain visible to the responsible IP reviewers.

Provenance requirements grow with the scope of generation. Engineers can review a generated leaf module line by line and scan it for token-level similarity, and swept values such as cache depths carry little copyright risk of their own, which moves legal review to the data used to train performance surrogates. If an autonomous design system generated multi-tier microarchitectural logic across millions of netlist lines, visual inspection could not detect semantic memorization or copyright infringement. Structural refactoring, signal renaming, and logic synthesis can disguise copylefted source logic from simple string scanners. Governance for such a system would therefore need lineage records linking the prompt, model checkpoint, and random seed to every synthesized block, although, as the controls below note, such records establish what was supplied and produced rather than where an emitted fragment originated. It would also need restricted processing environments that keep proprietary foundry process design kit (PDK) rules and third-party commercial IP out of training corpora and external model contexts.

The engineering organization surrounds the design system with four complementary governance controls:

- **Prompt and lineage records**: Retain the supplied specifications, prompts, tool transcripts, and intermediate artifacts with version identities and integrity hashes. A hash such as SHA-256 detects whether an artifact changed and a digital signature authenticates its signer, but neither establishes the origin of all content emitted by a model. Restricting retrieval to approved specifications likewise limits the supplied context, and formal equivalence checking can establish correspondence to a reference under declared assumptions, yet neither proves training-data provenance or noninfringement.
- **Similarity and license screening**: Screen generated RTL for recognizable overlap with indexed source repositories and retain the findings for review. A clean scan covers only the sources and similarities the scanner can detect; it is not an origin guarantee.
- **Restricted processing environments**: Declare where foundry PDK rules, cell libraries, and internal protocols may be processed. Restrict tool and network access accordingly, and retain the execution and transfer records needed to check compliance with that boundary.
- **Third-party IP boundaries**: Pin vendor block versions and interface contracts, and limit automated modifications to the scope the organization has authorized. Where internals are unavailable or modification is prohibited, explore integration through the exposed interfaces. Boundary checks can reveal prohibited tool actions without establishing the full legal status of the resulting system.

These controls make the technical history reviewable. IP acceptance and any indemnification decision still require the organization's separate review; passing functional checks cannot supply that decision.

### Managing Residual Risk with Hardware Chicken-Bits

Just as passing functional checks cannot settle IP provenance, it cannot eliminate every physical or microarchitectural uncertainty before freeze. Committing under uncertainty requires understanding failure modes well enough to accept, mitigate, or block them. Residual risk is an inherent technical property of a decision, not an administrative label. Usable residual risk statements specify five core elements:

1. **Failure mode**: explicit physical mechanism (such as dynamic $IR$-drop[^fn-ir-drop-c11] power collapse during bursty tensor execution, asynchronous clock-domain crossing (CDC) metastability[^fn-metastability-c11] races, or data arriving too late to meet the receiving register's setup-time requirement on a path covered by a timing waiver).
2. **Consequence**: impact on performance, power, thermals, data integrity, or safety.
3. **Remaining uncertainty**: quantified bounds where available, and an explicit statement of what remains uncharacterized, such as the operating conditions under which the waived path can meet setup time.
4. **Detecting check**: empirical test, telemetry signal, or monitor assigned to observe the mode.
5. **Containment action**: proposed fallback path, throttling mechanism, or hardware chicken-bit, with its verification status. If no containment is provided, state that explicitly and explain the basis for accepting the risk.

[^fn-ir-drop-c11]: **Resistive voltage drop and IR drop**: Resistive voltage drop ($V = I \times R$) occurs as current flows through the resistive metal wires of a chip's power delivery network. Dynamic $IR$ drop compounds this effect during simultaneous switching activity, causing localized supply voltage dips that increase gate propagation delays and can induce setup timing violations.

[^fn-metastability-c11]: **Clock domain crossing metastability**: A flip-flop may enter a metastable state and take unbounded time to resolve to a stable logic level when its input violates setup- or hold-time requirements during asynchronous clock domain crossings. If downstream logic samples the unresolved output, it can capture inconsistent logic values that cause system deadlocks.

Containment must address failure mechanisms that the original checks may not have covered. Spectre and Meltdown demonstrated information leakage through transient execution and microarchitectural side effects even when the forbidden computation did not become an architectural result [@KocherEtAl2019Spectre; @LippEtAl2018Meltdown]. Functional checks therefore cannot substitute for security properties that observe those effects. Whether a post-silicon control can mitigate a particular exposure depends on its behavior under that exposure and on the cost of the resulting operating mode.

In hardware design, containment controls can be permanent or reconfigurable. One-time-programmable e-fuses store configuration bits that supporting circuitry reads at power-on to select the corresponding behavior,[^fn-efuses-c11] such as loading memory-repair information into redundancy registers [@CostaBeerla2021EFuseRepair]. Firmware-managed chicken-bits,[^fn-chicken-bits-c11] by contrast, use privileged control registers to select implemented fallback modes such as disabling a speculative path or bounding throughput in instructions per cycle (IPC). Because synthesis and implementation must preserve any mode the product relies on, verification has to exercise both the nominal and asserted states to confirm that optimization left the fallback intact. The Lighthouse teaching example in @lst-ch11-chicken-bits distinguishes proposed control behavior from the mitigation that would still need to be demonstrated, while noting that these controls have not been implemented or measured in the retained study and that their costs and verification results remain open.

[^fn-chicken-bits-c11]: **Hardware chicken-bits and the dead-code elimination risk**: In semiconductor industry practice, a 'chicken-bit' is a dedicated configuration register that disables a high-risk microarchitectural optimization (such as speculative store-forwarding, aggressive prefetching, or deep out-of-order execution) if unforeseen physical defects appear post-tapeout. Automated synthesis and optimization tools face a critical hazard here: aggressive constant-propagation and dead-code elimination passes can treat fallback multiplexer branches as redundant logic and optimize them away. Implementation flows must preserve the specified fallback behavior and verify both nominal and asserted states. Retention constraints such as `set_dont_touch` may help where the flow requires them, but they do not replace a correct specification or implementation equivalence checks.

[^fn-efuses-c11]: **One-time-programmable e-fuses and wafer sort**: Electrically programmable fuses (e-fuses) store permanent, one-time-programmable configuration data during wafer sort or package test; on-chip logic reads those bits at power-on to configure redundant memory columns or disable flawed execution units [@CostaBeerla2021EFuseRepair]. A programmed fuse selects behavior the physical hardware already implements, whereas a post-silicon microcode patch requires dedicated SRAM patch storage and reload infrastructure.

One of those open costs is the performance penalty of running in a fallback mode. A commitment record for a speculative microarchitectural optimization should state the measured performance cost of its implemented fallback. For latency, a *derating penalty* compares nominal and derated execution under the same workload and operating conditions:[^fn-derating-penalty-c11]

$$
\Delta_{\text{derate}} = \frac{T_{\text{derated}} - T_{\text{nominal}}}{T_{\text{nominal}}}
$$

In @lst-ch11-chicken-bits, the penalty for `SLEW_RATE_LIMIT_NPU_BURSTS` remains unmeasured. Before relying on this proposed fallback, the commitment review must characterize its implemented behavior under the relevant failure mode and determine whether the 120\ FPS XR frame deadline and 3\ W TDP budget still hold under the measured derated envelope.

Programmable fallback controls also create a combinatorial verification problem. Implementing $N$ independent binary chicken-bits permits up to $2^N$ control configurations, which can make exhaustive verification difficult. Fallback paths can be overlooked when testbenches concentrate on nominal execution; when asserted in silicon, unexercised bypass logic can introduce livelocks, priority inversions, or bus deadlocks. The verification plan must cover the legal control combinations and their system interactions. Hierarchical proofs can help when their composition assumptions hold, but pairwise checks alone do not establish global deadlock freedom. The review must establish which controls can operate together and whether the resulting system preserves its required behavior.

```{.yaml #lst-ch11-chicken-bits lst-pos="tbp" lst-cap="**Proposed chicken-bit requirements.** Candidate fallback behavior, unmeasured costs, and checks still required before reliance."}
# Proposed controls; implementation and verification remain open
chicken_bits:
  fields:
    - name: DIS_SPEC_STORE_FWD
      nominal: 0  # Speculative store-to-load forwarding enabled
      fallback: 1 # Hold load issue until older uncommitted stores drain
      derate_penalty: "not measured"
      verification_status: "not run"
      required_check: "Ordering and progress under the RVWMO memory model"
    - name: FORCE_L1_WRITETHROUGH
      nominal: 0  # Write-back policy with dirty-line eviction
      fallback: 1 # Direct write-through to L2 cache to mitigate retention fault
      derate_penalty: "not measured"
      verification_status: "not run"
      required_check: "Retention-fault containment and memory-traffic effects"
    - name: SLEW_RATE_LIMIT_NPU_BURSTS
      nominal: 0  # Parallel MAC activation across accumulator columns
      fallback: 1 # Proposed staggered activation across MAC columns
      derate_penalty: "not measured"
      verification_status: "not run"
      required_check: "Dynamic voltage droop, correctness, and frame deadline"
```

[^fn-derating-penalty-c11]: **Microarchitectural derating penalty**: Silicon practitioners introduce derating factors to penalize nominal performance estimates when post-silicon workarounds (such as serialization or wait states) must be engaged to avoid physical timing violations, dynamic voltage droop, or race conditions under worst-case thermal and voltage corners.

Activating a slew-rate-limiting fallback could cause the candidate to miss its product target, and even passing the scoped derated check would establish only that the declared fallback stays within the requirements and conditions actually tested, not that the product is commercially viable or insulated from financial risk. The architect records that technical limit in the recommendation so that the named commitment authority can decide whether the remaining risk justifies tapeout.

Written out for the constructed Lighthouse case, the five elements read as one connected argument rather than a list. Peak $di/dt$[^fn-di-dt-c11] current transients during burst activation of the matrix accumulator array in dense GEMM execution could cause PDN voltage droop that threatens setup timing on high-activity matrix data paths, potentially corrupting calculations in downstream inference layers or forcing throttling that misses the proposed 120\ FPS operating point inside the 3\ W envelope. Because no dynamic $IR$-drop analysis has been run under the declared activity and package assumptions, the retained evidence bounds neither the droop magnitude and onset activity level nor the fallback's latency penalty and containment effectiveness. Candidate checks to detect this failure mode include dynamic $IR$-drop analysis before freeze, on-chip voltage droop monitors, post-silicon error-correcting code (ECC) syndrome logs and multi-bit error counts on the affected arrays, and NPU throttle and reset signatures, though the sensitivity of each check to this specific droop mode would itself need to be established. Relying on `SLEW_RATE_LIMIT_NPU_BURSTS` for containment would require verifying both its disabled and asserted states under the relevant droop conditions, checking its interaction with `FORCE_L1_WRITETHROUGH`, and showing that the derated envelope still holds the frame deadline. Where any detecting check remains unknown or a fallback unverified, the record must explain the consequence for the recommendation rather than treating the control as an established protection, and accepting a risk without containment requires stating why that risk is acceptable.

[^fn-di-dt-c11]: **Inductive voltage droop and current transients**: Inductive voltage droop ($V = L \cdot di/dt$) occurs across package and on-chip power distribution inductances when massive clock gating or simultaneous transistor switching causes rapid rates of change in current ($di/dt$). The resulting transient voltage drop can dip below SRAM minimum retention voltages, causing soft errors or logic failure.

The same discipline applies when a team wants to ship an uncharacterized feature disabled by default, such as a speculative vector turbo mode on an NPU. Retaining unverified circuitry on the die does not justify enabling it in production. A defensible exception requires a verified disabled state, an enable path restricted to authorized lab modes, verified reset and fault handling, proof that disabled circuitry does not violate baseline requirements, a named owner, and a firm expiration tied to post-silicon characterization. Unchecked exceptions risk normalizing deviance [@Vaughan1996Challenger], and the risk compounds once the components that generate candidates can also edit the files where exceptions are recorded.

One way to enforce this separation is to restrict the automated search loop to an isolated exploratory sandbox when evaluating speculative timing exceptions or constraint adjustments, while keeping the authoritative Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) files, UPF power-intent specifications, and waiver registries strictly read-only. The search loop can evaluate and rank candidates under candidate relaxations within its sandbox, but cannot promote waivers or SDC modifications to the release branch to make its own candidate close. In this example arrangement, each waiver, timing exception, and false-path declaration promoted to the release branch carries an out-of-band cryptographic signature from the responsible signoff specialist and is retained in a version-controlled record. The record states the technical justification, affected conditions, formal validation proofs, and what would require reconsideration. A temporary waiver also names its retirement criterion, such as a post-silicon characterization, a signoff-corner run, or a specific calendar milestone. The signature records who authorized the constraint change before a subsequent run relies on it; it does not establish that the exception is technically sound. A permanent exception may be justified by the design requirements, but its assumptions still need review when the design changes.

Whether a control disables an experimental mode or contains a post-silicon fault, every containment mechanism (hardware feature-disable fuses, firmware fallbacks, thermal derating modes, redundant UCIe lanes, memory isolation boundaries) requires checks matched to its failure mode. If an identified risk remains unacceptable and the design has no verified way to avoid or contain it, the candidate must not advance to tapeout. Not every residual risk requires a fallback, however; the recommendation must distinguish risks the organization can accept outright from those that require mitigation or redesign. For a proposed disable mechanism, the commitment review must verify the disabled state, isolate the failure from required behavior, and confirm that the control path remains available under the active fault being contained.

### Capital Allocation and Physical Qualification

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Errata study: every number in this section is read from the committed data in
# data/studies/01-silicon-errata-archaeology/ (errata_classified.csv, sources.csv,
# audit_metrics.json). Reproduce with the commands in that folder's README.
import csv
import json
from pathlib import Path

import _python.plots as _ap

_errata_dir = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "data/studies/01-silicon-errata-archaeology"
_errata = list(csv.DictReader((_errata_dir / "errata_classified.csv").open(encoding="utf-8")))
_sources = list(csv.DictReader(
    line for line in (_errata_dir / "sources.csv").open(encoding="utf-8") if not line.startswith("#")
))
_audit = json.loads((_errata_dir / "audit_metrics.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
_words = "zero one two three four five six seven eight nine ten eleven twelve".split()


def _pct(x):
    return f"{100 * x:.0f}"


def _ci(pair):
    return f"{100 * pair[0]:.0f} to {100 * pair[1]:.0f}"


errata_n = f"{len(_errata):,}"
families_n = len(_sources)
intel_families = sum(r["vendor"] == "Intel" for r in _sources)
amd_families = families_n - intel_families
unclassified_n = sum(r["subsystem"] == "Unclassified" for r in _errata)
audited_n = _audit["audited"]
agree_pct = _pct(_audit["agreement_weighted"])
agree_ci = _ci(_audit["agreement_weighted_ci95"])
failed_w = _words[len(_audit["failed_classes"])].capitalize()
rule_classes_w = _words[_audit["rule_classes"]]
_sh = _audit["shares"]
_mem = _sh["Memory controller, coherence fabric, and I/O"]
_core = _sh["Core execution, caches, and TLBs"]
_dbg = _sh["Debug, performance monitoring, and trace"]
mem_rule = f"{100 * _mem['rule_share']:.1f}"
mem_adj, mem_ci = _pct(_mem["adjusted_share"]), _ci(_mem["adjusted_ci95"])
core_adj, core_ci = _pct(_core["adjusted_share"]), _ci(_core["adjusted_ci95"])
dbg_adj, dbg_ci = _pct(_dbg["adjusted_share"]), _ci(_dbg["adjusted_ci95"])
arith_n = _words[_audit["arithmetic_datapath_audited"]]
arith_pct = f"{100 * _audit['arithmetic_datapath_share']:.0f}"
arith_ci = _ci(_audit["arithmetic_datapath_share_ci95"])
unique_titles = f"{_audit['unique_titles']:,}"
unique_mem = _pct(_audit["unique_title_shares"]["Memory controller, coherence fabric, and I/O"])
no_fix_pct = _pct(_audit["status_counts"]["No Fix"] / len(_errata))

# Composition of the largest reporting class, by rule label.
_by_rule = {}
for _r in _errata:
    _by_rule[_r["subsystem"]] = _by_rule.get(_r["subsystem"], 0) + 1
_io = _by_rule["I/O and peripheral interfaces"]
_mc = _by_rule["Memory controller and DRAM"]
_coh = _by_rule["Coherence and on-die or socket fabric"]
io_of_class_pct = _pct(_io / (_io + _mc + _coh))
memsys_rule_pct = f"{100 * (_mc + _coh + _by_rule['Caches, TLBs, and load-store ordering']) / len(_errata):.1f}"

# Vendor skew: the pooled shares are mostly Intel's documents.
intel_pct = _pct(sum(r["vendor"] == "Intel" for r in _errata) / len(_errata))
_amd = [r for r in _errata if r["vendor"] == "AMD"]
amd_n = len(_amd)
amd_mem_pct = _pct(sum(r["subsystem"] in (
    "I/O and peripheral interfaces", "Memory controller and DRAM",
    "Coherence and on-die or socket fabric") for r in _amd) / amd_n)

```

Advancing a candidate architecture from software simulation to physical silicon commits NRE capital for upfront mask costs and physical signoff.[^fn-mask-nre-c11] Faster candidate generation can compress front-end architecture exploration and initial logic synthesis, but it neither reduces the physical reticle mask charge for the selected process node nor eliminates post-silicon containment and derating costs. That cost structure implies, by inference rather than direct measurement, that accelerating front-end drafting leaves a larger share of the remaining financial and functional risk at the tapeout boundary. Published processor errata show where defects that survived pre-silicon verification were later documented, since Intel and AMD publish a specification update or revision guide for each processor family that itemizes the errata found after release. An analysis of the current documents covers `{python} families_n` families, `{python} intel_families` from Intel and `{python} amd_families` from AMD [@Intel2022XeonE5v4SpecUpdate; @Intel2020XeonScalableSpecUpdate; @Intel2023XeonScalableGen2SpecUpdate; @Intel2026XeonScalableGen3SpecUpdate; @Intel2026XeonScalableGen4SpecUpdate; @Intel2026XeonScalableGen5SpecUpdate; @Intel2025Core8th9thGenSpecUpdate; @Intel2026Core10thGenSpecUpdate; @Intel2026Core11thGenTigerLakeSpecUpdate; @Intel2023Core11thGenRocketLakeSpecUpdate; @Intel2026Core12thGenSpecUpdate; @Intel2026Core13th14thGenSpecUpdate; @Intel2026CoreUltraSpecUpdate; @Intel2026CoreUltra200VSpecUpdate; @Intel2026CoreUltraSeries2SpecUpdate; @AMD2023Family17h00hRevisionGuide; @AMD2026Family17h30hRevisionGuide; @AMD2025Family19h10hRevisionGuide; @AMD2025Family1Ah00hRevisionGuide], and across all `{python} errata_n` itemized errata the entries recovered from each document's detailed errata section match its summary table, erratum for erratum.

[^fn-mask-nre-c11]: **Mask tooling non-recurring engineering and physical signoff**: A reticle mask set is an upfront capital expenditure, with one photomask for each patterned layer, paid before any production wafer is processed. One analyst estimate puts a mask set above \$1 million at 28\ nm, above \$10 million at 7\ nm, and near \$40 million approaching 3\ nm [@Patel2022MaskSetCosts]. Faster automated exploration does not reduce this charge for a chosen node, and a respin that changes many layers pays much of it again, along with months of fabrication delay.

A familiar expectation concerns where those escapes might cluster. Memory controllers, coherence fabrics, and caches cross asynchronous clock domains, arbitrate shared resources, and admit many interleavings of concurrent requests, which can make their verification state spaces large. That complexity would lead us to look for a concentration of published escapes in these subsystems. Arithmetic units have comparatively compact specifications and mature formal checks, suggesting fewer published escapes. Assigning errata to subsystems can describe the resulting distribution, although counts alone cannot measure verification difficulty or the probability of an escape.

Assigning each erratum to a subsystem takes judgment, so our classification pairs a committed keyword rule set with a stratified audit (@fig-errata-subsystem-shares). The rules match whole words and phrases in an erratum's title, fall back to its problem statement when the title matches nothing, and use no default bucket, leaving `{python} unclassified_n` unmatched errata unclassified. We then audited a seeded, stratified random sample of `{python} audited_n` errata using a model-assisted reading of the extracted problem and implication text, a check that shares the co-generation limitation warned about in @sec-stronger-evaluation-expensive and @sec-independent-checks-and-correlated-errors because the same model family helped draft the rules and label the sample. The rules agree with that reading on an estimated `{python} agree_pct`% of all errata (95% interval `{python} agree_ci`%), but `{python} failed_w` of the initial `{python} rule_classes_w` rule classes fell short of the required precision and were either merged with adjacent classes they were confused with or folded into the unclassified bar.[^fn-errata-audit-c11]

[^fn-errata-audit-c11]: **Errata classification audit and class consolidation**: Even when each erratum's rule label is hidden from the audit worksheet, a model-assisted audit shares assumptions with model-drafted keyword rules. In that audit, caches and translation lookaside buffers (TLBs), coherence fabrics, and security features were merged with the adjacent classes they were most often confused with, while the machine-check reporting class and the graphics and accelerator class fell below the precision threshold and were folded into the unclassified total. Supplying an independent reference would require a human reviewer labeling the same stratified sample blind to both the rule and model labels, using Cohen's $\kappa$ to measure agreement beyond chance before estimating adjusted shares; that blind human relabeling has not yet been performed.

![**Published CPU errata spread across subsystems; no reported class holds much more than a fifth.** Shares of `{python} errata_n` errata from the specification updates and revision guides of `{python} families_n` Intel and AMD CPU families, grouped by committed keyword rules into six reported classes. The largest class is mostly I/O and peripheral errata. Bars give the rule-assigned share; dots and whiskers give the share adjusted by a model-assisted audit of a stratified sample of `{python} audited_n` errata, with 95% intervals. The hatched bar holds errata that no rule matched and two classes that failed the audit.](images/fig-errata-subsystem-shares){#fig-errata-subsystem-shares width="100%" fig-alt="Horizontal bar chart of published CPU errata shares for six subsystem classes and a hatched bar for errata not resolved to a class. I/O with memory controllers and coherence, debug and performance monitoring, and core execution with caches and TLBs have bars of similar length, virtualization and security is somewhat shorter, and power and interrupts are the shortest. Each bar carries a dot with an interval marking an audit-adjusted estimate that overlaps the bars of neighboring classes."}

Although the largest reported class merges I/O and peripheral interfaces with memory controllers and coherence fabrics (`{python} mem_rule`% of the errata by rule and an estimated `{python} mem_adj`% after the audit, 95% interval `{python} mem_ci`%), `{python} io_of_class_pct`% of its entries by rule are I/O and peripheral errata. Memory controllers, coherence fabrics, and caches, the logic the state-space argument singles out, account for `{python} memsys_rule_pct`% by rule and do not dominate the published errata within this classification. Core execution, caches, and TLBs hold a comparable audit-adjusted share of `{python} core_adj`% (`{python} core_ci`%), while the logic that observes execution, meaning performance counters, trace, and debug exceptions, holds another `{python} dbg_adj`% (`{python} dbg_ci`%). Arithmetic datapath errata are uncommon in the audit sample: only `{python} arith_n` of the `{python} audited_n` audited errata describe a floating-point, integer, or vector unit that computes or schedules incorrectly, an estimated `{python} arith_pct`% of all errata (`{python} arith_ci`%). The documented behavior spans control and integration logic: virtualization and isolation features, power-state transitions, reset and interrupt flows, protocol compliance on I/O links, and the counters that watch all of them. Several of the audited errata sit where two such features meet. A VM entry that clears the trace-enable bit can emit a spurious trace packet [@Intel2020XeonScalableSpecUpdate], and after a C6 exit the processor can dispatch a queued interrupt before an earlier one of the same priority completes [@Intel2022XeonE5v4SpecUpdate].

Several limits bound this reading. A published erratum is a defect the vendor chose to document for customers, not a complete census of escapes. The shares also have no denominator. No document reports how much logic or specified behavior each subsystem contains, so a share cannot be normalized by subsystem size or complexity, and a large share cannot be interpreted as a higher escape rate. The classes differ in scope and were fixed after the audit, so an equal split among them is not a natural baseline. The pool is also mostly one vendor, since `{python} intel_pct`% of the errata come from Intel documents; in the `{python} amd_n` AMD errata alone, the I/O, memory-controller, and coherence class holds `{python} amd_mem_pct`% by rule. Finally, the documents overlap, because a defect in shared logic appears in every family that inherits it; counting each distinct title once leaves `{python} unique_titles` errata and puts that class at `{python} unique_mem`%.

The counts support a descriptive observation rather than a test of the state-space explanation. Arithmetic units have compact specifications against which equivalence checking, formal proof, and dense random testing are well established, although the Pentium division flaw shows that they are not immune [@Edelman1997PentiumDivision], and published arithmetic errata are rare. Memory subsystems and platform interconnects cross asynchronous clock domains, arbitrate shared buses, and admit many cache-coherence interleavings, yet the chosen categories place substantial shares of these documents' errata elsewhere too. One reading consistent with these counts, though not established by them, is that escapes follow the breadth of specified behavior, meaning logic whose correct response depends on many architectural modes, power states, and feature interactions at once, wherever on the die it sits.

Specification updates also record whether a fix is planned or has been made, and `{python} no_fix_pct`% of the errata in this corpus carry no planned fix. Because the study records the least resolved disposition whenever a document gives different dispositions across steppings, that percentage describes published entries across the covered variants rather than the fraction of shipped processors with an active defect or the availability of a usable workaround. Any workaround proposed for a commitment still needs its own functional checks and measured performance cost under the conditions in which it will be used.

That dispersion across subsystems bears directly on front-end productivity claims. Assistance confined to drafting an arithmetic leaf block does not touch the broader control and integration behavior represented in these documents, though the counts identify only the scope that design and verification work must cover rather than measuring escape risk or showing how generated RTL would compare with human-written RTL. Whereas parameter tuning inside a fixed container cannot by itself re-architect a power-state sequence or a bus protocol, a system that generated the control and integration logic across which these errata are spread, including interconnect fabrics, power-state sequencing, virtualization support, and the counters and trace that observe them, would be working where those escapes occur. To determine whether broader generation increases or reduces defect escapes, a comparative study must pair contract verification and physical checks matched to the generated scope with evidence for any fallback on which the recommendation relies, since manual code review alone cannot establish those properties.

The workflow comparison and the product decision therefore need separate accounts. For the evidence test in @sec-moonshot, added verification work may be justified by a better architecture result, offset by savings elsewhere, or large enough to erase the claimed advantage. A matched comparison of the complete approaches must resolve that question within the assessed scope. A simulator-level study can support such a comparison without delivering a silicon-ready design.

For the commitment test, the organization asks whether the particular product justifies the remaining expenditure and risk. Expected shipment volume affects how the program can recover its NRE (@sec-design-cost-pressure), while physical qualification determines whether the candidate is ready for the proposed transition. A workflow may demonstrate an advantage even when its resulting product is unaffordable; a product may justify commitment even when no AI-native workflow advantage has been established. Keeping these judgments separate prevents an attractive cost story from supplying missing technical evidence.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="The Lighthouse commitment remains open"}
**Context.** Freezing a Level-2 cache capacity or selecting an accelerator organization for the Lighthouse mobile XR subsystem would constrain later software, memory, and physical implementation choices.

**Application.** The prospective cache study halted before dispatch, and the executed array study evaluated only isolated GEMM cycles. Neither record provides the physical signoff, power modeling, or system-level checks required to authorize silicon implementation.

**Outcome.** The supported recommendation is to obtain the missing system evidence before advancing toward freeze or tapeout. The person responsible for the product would still need to assess the resulting recommendation across all eight requirement domains (@sec-intent-vs-spec) and record a decision.
:::

A tapeout plan for the Lighthouse implementation requires integrating five distinct classes of qualified specialist evidence:

1. **Physical verification**: design rule check (DRC), layout versus schematic (LVS), antenna ratio checks, electrical rule checks for electrostatic discharge (ESD) and latchup immunity, and design-for-manufacturing dummy metal density and chemical-mechanical polishing planarity rules against selected foundry decks, recording deck identities, approved waivers, and unresolved violations.
2. **Timing qualification**: setup and hold analysis across declared process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners, extraction modes, and variation models.
3. **Power integrity, thermal, and packaging reliability qualification**: dynamic and static voltage-drop ($IR$ drop), electromigration (EM), spatial thermal dissipation under workload traces, and thermo-mechanical stress analysis (evaluating thermal expansion mismatch and microbump strain across 2.5D packaging substrates) under declared activity and packaging assumptions.
4. **Logic and implementation correspondence**: formal equivalence checking stating compared representations, assumptions, and out-of-proof transformations.
5. **Manufacturing test qualification**: design-for-test (DFT) and automatic test pattern generation (ATPG) coverage metrics against manufacturing-test targets, identifying fault models and residual coverage gaps.

Passing those technical checks still does not establish the right to use a design or resolve the organization's legal obligations, which require a separate review of the applicable sources, licenses, contracts, and jurisdictions. Because neither technical nor legal review grants commitment authority on its own, missing required evidence blocks a recommendation to advance, while an eligible design still goes to the named commitment authority to decide whether to proceed or return for further physical qualification.

## Sustaining Architectural Ownership {#sec-sustaining-responsibility}

Authorizing a tapeout does not end the architect's responsibility for the design. Architectural ownership is the active capability to question and reopen design decisions throughout the system life cycle, which requires preserving access to candidates, boundary constraints, rejected alternatives, simulation traces, and signoff reports spanning compute, interconnect, memory, and packaging subsystems. Naming reviewers who lack access to decisive artifacts or the ability to stop an unsupported decision creates a mismatch between responsibility and control, where people with limited control over automated systems become what Elish calls moral crumple zones[^fn-crumple-c11] when the system fails [@Elish2019MoralCrumpleZones]. In hardware organizations, the immediate concern is that a named reviewer may be unable to investigate the result they are expected to endorse, while research on automation bias further warns against replacing independent examination with reliance on automated recommendations [@SkitkaEtAl1999AutomationBias].

That mismatch grows with the scope of generation. When engineers write and integrate the modules themselves, or set an optimizer's parameter ranges and validate its surrogate, holding them responsible for defect escapes matches their control. If an autonomous system generated millions of register-transfer lines across complex cross-layer hierarchies, requiring a human engineer to sign off on the design by inspecting raw RTL would be an organizational fiction. No human can detect subtle asynchronous races or timing exceptions across millions of machine-synthesized gates through visual review. An organization that mandates human signoff on uninspectable code merely positions the engineer to absorb blame when physical defects escape into silicon.

Sustaining authentic ownership in such a workflow requires aligning the signoff surface with human capability rather than asking architects to verify line-level syntax they did not draft. Ownership shifts to the input specifications, formal correctness contracts, physical signoff reports, and fallback derating envelopes: the architect answers for the completeness of the constraints and the rigor of the evaluation harness, while physical signoff checks backed by immutable execution records establish whether the candidate satisfies those requirements under the analyzed conditions.

[^fn-crumple-c11]: **Moral crumple zones**: Elish's term for human operators who bear responsibility for an automated system's failure despite having limited control over its autonomous behavior [@Elish2019MoralCrumpleZones]. It describes an organizational mismatch between responsibility and operational control, not a rule assigning legal liability.

Retaining access to those records and models matters just as much after mask release. Archiving the simulation infrastructure and cross-layer models without a usable way to run them leaves operating teams with symptoms they cannot trace back to the design assumptions. Diagnostic capability therefore belongs in the handoff to the team responsible for the deployed system.
