Keeping that diagnostic capability sharp requires deliberate practice before and after handoff. Engineers stay ready to challenge a recommendation when they reproduce selective checks, inspect failed candidates, and diagnose seeded logic and timing faults in CPU and NPU blocks on their own before viewing tool recommendations, which reveals gaps in the team's understanding. Because opaque external dependencies (black-box IP blocks, foundry PDKs, commercial EDA engines) can also hide failure mechanisms without absolving engineering responsibility, tapeout commitments must record IP versions, interface invariants, independent cross-checks, and hard-to-diagnose failure modes so that a vendor certificate never substitutes for an independent technical check.

When architectural responsibility passes from the design team to post-silicon bring-up or operations, the handoff must include that underlying technical basis:

1. **Candidate release identity and boundary**: stated design question, system boundaries, and baseline assumptions.
2. **Results and reproducible checks**: passed, failed, inconclusive, and missing results across CPU, NPU, memory, and packaging layers, together with the models, inputs, tool versions, and access needed to rerun decisive checks. Checks the receiving team cannot reproduce need an identified route to the specialist or supplier who can investigate them.
3. **Uncertainty and containment**: bounded remaining uncertainties and validated fallback paths.
4. **Invalidation conditions**: explicit shifts in workloads, software stacks, EDA versions, manufacturing processes, or interfaces that mandate reconsideration.

The transferred technical basis guides monitoring priorities. Where the system exposes them, operating teams can track CPU queue tail latencies, UCIe retry rates, LPDDR5 ECC error counts, NPU thermal throttling, and reset signatures. These signals become useful for architectural diagnosis when tied to conditions on which the recommendation depended. For example, if sustained NPU throughput was evaluated under an assumed thermal envelope, observed throttling calls for checking workload, cooling, and operating conditions against that envelope before revising the throughput conclusion.

Any party with access to the record may raise an invalidation condition, while the architect of record or a designated successor is responsible for reopening the technical recommendation and the person authorized to make the product decision is responsible for reconsidering the commitment that rested on it. When a trigger arises from a telemetry signal outside a declared operating condition, a workload or interface change that meets an invalidation condition, or a qualified check that contradicts a relied-upon result, the team must connect that observation to the recommendation's assumptions. Reopening appends a dated entry naming the trigger, who raised it, and any revised recommendation and decision rather than editing the history in place, so that the original recommendation, decision, and evidence stand as written.

## Architectural Alignment Under Team Churn {#sec-sustaining-alignment-churn}

Invalidation triggers do not arise only after silicon returns from the foundry; an architectural recommendation must also remain valid while distributed teams actively change the design. When engineers and automated loops push daily commits to RTL repositories, device drivers, compiler backends, and firmware stacks, a recommendation built on last month's repository snapshot can quietly go stale. The team needs a reliable way to see which changes affect the recommendation and which results must be checked again.

To keep the recommendation anchored as the repository moves, the architect ties each recommendation to a specific integration snapshot and states which changes require rerunning its checks. Continuous integration then runs equivalence, timing, and interface checks at a fidelity matched to each changed artifact, while full physical qualification covers the integrated candidate that reaches commitment review. When delegating subblock optimization, the architect also specifies which external bus protocols, clock-domain crossings, and register-map addresses must remain fixed. Because such modification boundaries narrow the scope of a change without guaranteeing a clean merge or preserving physical validity, the integrated candidate must still be checked for cross-block interactions that a local comparison could not observe.

Even on a fixed repository snapshot, run-to-run variation requires diagnosis before a candidate can advance. If an automated tuning pass produces high-performing RTL on one seed but fails timing closure or routability on another, the architect must first determine whether the generator produced different candidates across seeds or whether repeated implementation runs of the same candidate exposed marginal physical closure. Whereas the first points to an unstable search, the second points to a candidate operating too close to a timing or congestion cliff, so the recommendation must state which source of variation was tested and under what conditions. When unexpected failures still escape into silicon, they force commitments open again, as the Pentium FDIV bug [@Edelman1997PentiumDivision] showed by invalidating release confidence and demanding renewed architecture work, containment, and a recall or replacement decision.

## Closing the Moonshot {#sec-closing-moonshot}

This book opened with an ambition stated in one breath: design a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for a real-time mobile XR workload. That prompt anchored the running Lighthouse study across the preceding chapters as we traced how an architect turns an underspecified goal into explicit requirements, chooses representations and methods, runs simulators and physical-design tools, checks what their feedback actually proves, transfers lessons across the stack, and evaluates the complete workflow.

The book's own records establish a concrete finding when evaluated against the operational layers. The prospective cache study (@sec-architecture-20-ontology and @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces) was set up to sweep cache capacities within a fixed structural container, but it stopped before tool dispatch because the required implementation, measurement, and dispatch setup remained incomplete. While the separate executed array study evaluated isolated GEMM cycle counts on synthetic kernels and retained a local tie across array parameters $\theta \in \Theta$, that pre-registered sweep left the structural container $\Theta$ frozen, altered no plan in response to returned results, and engaged no physical feedback, so it neither completes the prospective cache study nor demonstrates an adaptive design loop. Neither study approached the Layer 3 ambition of the Architecture 2.0 moonshot, which would require opening the structural container to co-design RV64GCV CPU extensions, NPU matrix datapaths, MLIR compiler lowering schedules, and UCIe packaging links against physical signoff tools, and neither record establishes the physical or software feasibility of the Lighthouse subsystem.

Against the two closing tests, the verdict is plain:

1. **Program claim status.** Against the first test, the Lighthouse program claim is *unresolved* because the retained records do not compare a complete AI-native approach with a credible alternative at matched scope and budget, establishing neither an improvement in the architecture result nor a reduction in total cost to reach a comparable result. Adding physical measurements alone would not settle this claim, since the comparative workflow evidence would still be needed.
2. **Architecture commitment.** Against the second test, no tapeout commitment packet was authorized or submitted. The required implementation evidence, including physical timing, power delivery, software integration, and verified containment, is absent. The supported recommendation remains to obtain that evidence before advancing. A named commitment authority would still have to decide whether the resulting trade-offs and residual risk justify tapeout, even if every required technical check passed.

This book's contribution is a way to reason systematically about design work while the program-level outcome remains open. The Lighthouse case makes the missing evidence concrete, and the separate array study shows how even a tie can narrow a local architecture question. Readers can apply the same discipline to a new problem: choose representations and methods, develop alternative organizations, use feedback to revise them, examine what the tools actually measured, compare the complete approaches, and state what remains necessary for commitment. Later evidence may support or reject an AI-native advantage.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Delegate Execution, Retain Accountability"}
**The principle:** As automated design systems generate alternatives, explore, optimize, and synthesize across the stack, architects remain responsible for framing the problem, selecting abstractions, resolving cross-layer tradeoffs, interpreting results, and supporting the technical recommendation. A named commitment authority remains accountable for deciding whether the organization makes an irreversible capital commitment.

**The application:** Tie each recommendation to the implementation and conditions its evidence covers, and state what would require reconsidering it. Before an irreversible commitment, identify the responsible decision maker, declare the residual risks, and verify any containment paths on which the recommendation relies.
:::

## Open Questions

Separating the technical recommendation from commitment authority makes it clear who is accountable for a silicon decision, but exercising that judgment across complex, machine-generated designs leaves several open research questions:

- **How can an architect diagnose failures across third-party chiplets when vendors will not share their internal RTL?** In a multi-die package connected over Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe), an intermittent deadlock or tail-latency spike may start in a host CPU coherence controller, an interposer link, or a third-party accelerator direct memory access (DMA) engine. Because commercial chiplet vendors rarely disclose their internal register-transfer logic, the team integrating the package must track down faults across black-box boundaries. We still lack standard interface contracts and minimal boundary telemetry that let an integrator pinpoint which die violated a protocol or power-delivery assumption without exposing proprietary circuit details.

- **How do we design and verify post-silicon chicken-bits when $N$ independent switches create $2^N$ operating modes?** Hardware chicken-bits and dynamic throttling modes give teams a way to work around unmodeled voltage droop or subtle coherence races after tapeout, yet $N$ independent binary overrides create $2^N$ operating configurations that can introduce new deadlocks or push latency past the product's derating budget ($\Delta_{\text{derate}}$) when asserted together. Architects still need synthesis and formal verification methods that can build small sets of mutually compatible fallback modes and prove that every reachable derated mode stays free of deadlocks and meets declared real-time deadlines.

- **How can signoff tools catch cases where several locally safe waivers combine to break the system?** During late-stage timing and physical closure, specialists routinely approve isolated exceptions, such as a multi-cycle timing path in a datapath, a local dynamic $IR$-drop margin waiver on a memory stripe, and a firmware-restricted turbo mode. Even when each waiver is sound under its own local assumptions, triggering several of them at once during concurrent workload bursts can push the integrated chip past its thermal or timing limit, much as post-incident investigations in aerospace and nuclear engineering repeatedly trace system failures to accumulated maintenance waivers whose cross-subsystem interactions were never checked together. Signoff flows still lack a practical way to combine timing, power-intent, and firmware constraints into shared contracts that automatically flag mutually incompatible waivers as revisions accumulate.

- **What should a design tool show an architect so that reviewing a generated design builds diagnostic understanding rather than rubber-stamp approval?** When automated loops take over routine floorplanning and pipeline tuning, engineers lose the line-by-line debugging practice that builds structural intuition, creating the conditions for automation bias and moral crumple zones. Neither summary scorecards nor dumps of raw tool logs solve that problem. We need tools that can isolate the shortest execution trace or the smallest shift in physical constraints or workload phase that causes a recommended design to fail, so the architect can see directly where its margins break down.

- **How can we tell whether generated RTL copied a protected circuit design after synthesis and renaming have changed all the signal and module names?** Before committing capital to mask fabrication, an organization must be confident that generated register-transfer logic does not infringe third-party intellectual property or leak restricted foundry design rules. Standard text and token scanners fail on hardware descriptions because canonical Boolean optimization, retiming, and signal renaming rewrite surface syntax while preserving the underlying state machine or datapath organization. We still lack graph-level and formal-equivalence provenance checks that can bound structural memorization against training corpora without requiring vendors to disclose proprietary IP libraries.

## Summary

Architects contribute by choosing problems worth solving, selecting useful abstractions, identifying omitted constraints, and connecting workload and software behavior to physical consequences. An AI-native design system may generate alternatives and use feedback to redesign them, but those capabilities do not remove the need for a supported system recommendation or for an accountable person to make the product decision.

Ownership therefore connects technical judgment to continuing responsibility. Domain specialists qualify individual results, the architect reconciles them into a system recommendation, and a named decision maker within an accountable organization decides whether to advance. Because later changes to the software, implementation, workload, or observed silicon behavior can invalidate the basis of that decision, keeping diagnostic tools, reviewable records, and verified containment paths available lets the responsible teams reopen the recommendation when conditions change.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Own the architecture problem.** The architect connects mechanisms, interfaces, software, and physical constraints into a system recommendation. This includes choosing abstractions, identifying omitted effects that could reverse a decision, and determining when feedback calls for a different organization rather than further tuning of the current one.
- **Investigate discrepancies.** Align the assumptions and conditions behind specialist results, then select observations that can distinguish possible causes of disagreement. Scoped support informs the system recommendation; a named authority separately decides whether to advance. Parallel exploration does not itself authorize changes to the requirements.
- **Check derating and chicken-bit containment.** Proposed chicken-bits require a verified safe state, empirical characterization of the implemented control's performance penalty, compatible control combinations, and checks that the candidate preserves the declared requirements under the tested derated envelope ($\Delta_{\text{derate}}$).
- **Recheck results as the design changes.** Tie the recommendation to an identified integration version, state which interfaces a delegated change must preserve, and recheck affected results before relying on the revised design.
:::

Much of the evidence an architect needs to support those recommendations depends on shared resources beyond any single team: access to qualified physical-design flows, comparable evaluations, and diagnostic experience that survives increased automation. In @sec-bootstrapping-ecosystem, we examine what the discipline must build together to make that evidence more accessible.
